title: How Investors Should Hire and Manage a Rehab Contractor
metaDescription: What investors should ask a renovation contractor, how to compare bids apples to apples, how to verify license and insurance, and set updates and warranties.
h1: Working with a Renovation Contractor as an Investor: Questions, Bids, Checks and Communication
dek: Investors get the best results from contractors when the relationship is built on a detailed scope, bids that can be compared line by line, verified licensing and insurance, payment tied to completed work, a regular reporting cadence and a written warranty. Most contractor problems trace back to skipping one of those steps.
keyTakeaways: Ask contractors about investor work specifically: draws, documentation, remote reporting, permits and how they handle hidden conditions.
Bids can only be compared when every contractor prices the same written scope, with the same allowances, exclusions and finish levels.
Verify licensing, general liability and workers' compensation insurance directly, and ask to be named as an additional insured where appropriate.
Tie payments to completed, verified work and collect lien waivers with every draw.
Agree on communication cadence, change-order process and warranty terms before work begins, in writing.

sections.h2: How is hiring a contractor different for an investor than for a homeowner?
sections.body:
A homeowner hiring a contractor usually focuses on design, finish quality and living through the project. An investor needs those things too, but the priorities are different.

You care about the numbers. The rehab budget is a direct input into your return, so cost predictability matters as much as cost itself. A contractor who bids low and fills the gap with change orders can be more expensive than one who bids completely.

You care about the clock. Every day the house is under construction adds holding costs, so reliability on schedule is worth paying for.

You may not be on site. Many investors own properties in markets they do not live in, or own enough properties that they cannot visit each one regularly. You need a contractor who documents progress and communicates clearly without being prompted.

You need paperwork. Lenders want draw requests and inspections. Buyers, appraisers and future lenders want permits finaled. Title companies want lien waivers. Insurers want proof of coverage. A contractor who treats documentation as part of the job saves you trouble at every exit.

You may be doing this again. A contractor who understands your finish standard, your exit strategies and your communication preferences becomes more valuable with every project.

That means the evaluation goes beyond price and portfolio photos. You are evaluating a working relationship and a process, not only the quality of a finished kitchen.

sections.h2: What questions should you ask a renovation contractor?
sections.body:
Ask questions that require specific answers and reveal how the contractor actually operates.

About experience:
- What share of your work is for investors, and what types: flips, rentals, BRRRR, multifamily, bank-owned properties?
- Can you show recent projects similar to this one, with references from investor clients?
- Have you worked on houses of this era and construction type in this area?

About process:
- Who will manage this project day to day, and how often will that person be on site?
- Do you use your own crews, subcontractors, or both? How do you vet subcontractors?
- How do you handle permits and inspections, and who pulls them?
- How do you handle hidden conditions and change orders? Can I see a sample change order?
- How do you schedule trades, and how do you handle material lead times?

About money:
- What is your payment structure? Do you require a deposit, and if so, how much and for what?
- How do your draws line up with completed work, and can you work with my lender's draw process?
- Do you provide lien waivers from yourself and your subcontractors and suppliers with each draw?
- Are dumpsters, debris removal and cleanup included?

About communication and documentation:
- How will you report progress, and how often?
- Will I get photos and video at each stage, including before walls close?
- What documentation will I receive at completion?

About quality and warranty:
- What warranty do you provide, on what, for how long, and what is excluded?
- How do you handle punch list items and callbacks?

The answers show whether the contractor has a process or improvises one for each job.

sections.h2: How do you compare bids apples to apples?
sections.body:
Bids are only comparable if they price the same work. The most common mistake investors make is comparing totals from contractors who each wrote their own scope, then hiring the lowest number.

Start with a written scope you control. It should cover each room or system, what work is being done, the finish level or specific products, quantities where they matter, allowances for items not yet selected, and explicit exclusions. Send the same scope to every bidder and ask them to price it as written, noting any items they believe are missing or wrong.

When bids come back, compare them line by line:
- Did each contractor price every item in the scope?
- Are allowances the same in every bid? A low bid with low allowances may become the highest bid after selections.
- Are permits, inspections, dumpsters, debris removal and final cleaning included?
- Are there exclusions one bid lists that others do not, such as hazardous materials, sewer work, or repairs behind walls?
- Is any contractor's price for a major item far out of line with the others? An unusually low line item may mean a misunderstanding of the work.
- What are the payment terms and draw schedule?
- What warranty is included?
- What schedule does each contractor commit to?

Ask the low and high bidders to walk you through their pricing. Often the difference is in scope interpretation, not efficiency. A contractor who asks good questions about the scope during bidding is usually one who will manage the project well.

Genstone's estimates are built as a detailed scope document with labor, materials and a draw schedule, which is the kind of format that makes line-by-line comparison possible.

sections.h2: How do you verify licensing and insurance?
sections.body:
Verification takes a short time and protects against some of the most serious risks in renovation.

Licensing. Contractor licensing is set by states and sometimes cities and counties. Some states license general contractors; others license only certain trades such as electrical, plumbing and HVAC; some require registration rather than a license. Check what applies where the property is, then look up the contractor's license or registration on the licensing agency's public website. Confirm the license is active, in the company's name, in the right category for the work, and check for disciplinary actions or complaints. For pre-1978 houses, confirm the firm's EPA lead-safe RRP certification as well.

Insurance. Ask for certificates of insurance sent directly from the contractor's insurance agent, not a copy the contractor hands you. Confirm:
- General liability coverage, with limits appropriate to the project
- Workers' compensation coverage for employees, as required by the state, or documentation of any legitimate exemption
- Commercial auto coverage for company vehicles
- That policies are current and will remain in force through the project

Where appropriate, ask to be named as an additional insured on the contractor's general liability policy. Talk with your own insurance agent about what you need and about your builder's risk or vacant dwelling coverage during the rehab.

Subcontractors. If the contractor uses subcontractors, ask how they verify their licenses and insurance. An uninsured subcontractor injured on your property can create exposure for you.

Keep copies of all licenses and certificates in the property file. Lenders and institutional buyers may ask for them.

sections.h2: How should payment and draws be structured?
sections.body:
Payment structure is one of the most important protections in a renovation contract. The principle is simple: pay for work that has been completed and verified.

Avoid large upfront payments. Some contractors request a deposit to cover mobilization or special-order materials. Where a deposit is needed, it should be modest, tied to specific purposes, and consistent with any state rules that limit deposits on home improvement contracts. Large deposits leave you exposed if the contractor fails to perform.

Tie draws to milestones. A draw schedule lists the stages of work and the payment due when each is complete, such as demolition complete, rough-ins passed inspection, drywall finished, cabinets and counters installed, and final completion. Each draw should be verified by your own inspection, photos or video, or your lender's inspector before payment.

Collect lien waivers. In many states, subcontractors and suppliers who are not paid can file liens against your property even if you paid the general contractor. With each draw, collect conditional or unconditional lien waivers from the contractor, and on larger jobs from major subcontractors and suppliers. At final payment, collect final waivers.

Hold back final payment until the work is complete and accepted. The final payment should follow final inspections, completion of the punch list, delivery of documentation and your approval.

Align with your lender. If you are using a rehab loan, the contractor's draw schedule should match the lender's draw milestones so funds release when work is verified.

Genstone works on this model: no upfront payment, construction draws tied to completed work, and final payment after completion and the client's approval, with lien waivers handled as part of the process.

sections.h2: What communication cadence works for investors?
sections.body:
Good communication is structured and predictable. It should tell you what you need to make decisions without requiring you to chase updates.

Agree on a cadence before work starts. A common pattern includes:
- A kickoff conversation to confirm scope, schedule, selections, access, the change-order process and points of contact
- Regular progress reports at a set interval, such as weekly, with photos or video, work completed, work planned next, upcoming inspections and any open decisions
- Immediate notification for hidden conditions, safety issues, failed inspections or anything that affects budget or schedule
- Milestone documentation at each draw, including photos before walls are closed
- A final walkthrough, in person or by video, followed by a punch list

Keep decisions in writing. Verbal conversations on site are fine, but confirm decisions by email, text or a project management tool so there is a record. This is especially important for change orders and selections.

Name a single point of contact on each side. A project manager who owns the schedule and communicates for the contractor, and one person on your side who can approve decisions, prevents mixed messages.

Respond quickly. The contractor's ability to keep the schedule depends partly on your speed. If you will be unavailable, designate someone who can make decisions.

For remote investors, photo and video documentation is the core of the relationship. Ask for photos of rough plumbing, electrical and framing before drywall, since those are the parts of the house you will never see again. A designated field manager who reports from the site is what makes remote ownership workable.

sections.h2: What should a renovation warranty cover?
sections.body:
A warranty is the contractor's commitment to correct defects in their work for a defined period after completion. Get it in writing and read it before signing the contract.

A clear warranty states:
- What is covered, typically defects in workmanship performed by the contractor and its subcontractors
- How long it lasts
- What is excluded, commonly normal wear and tear, damage by tenants or occupants, damage from lack of maintenance, owner-supplied materials, and work modified by others
- How to make a claim, and how quickly the contractor will respond
- How manufacturer warranties on materials and equipment are handled

Manufacturer warranties are separate. Roofing materials, windows, HVAC equipment, water heaters, appliances and some flooring carry manufacturer warranties, often with registration requirements. Ask the contractor to register equipment where needed and provide the documentation at completion. Some manufacturer warranties depend on proper installation by qualified installers.

For rentals, read the exclusions carefully. Most workmanship warranties exclude tenant damage, so you will need to distinguish between a defect in the work and damage from use. Good move-in documentation helps with this.

For flips, ask whether the warranty transfers to a buyer. A transferable warranty can be a modest selling point.

Genstone provides a one-year workmanship warranty, with tenant damage and normal wear excluded, which is a typical structure. Whatever the terms, keep the warranty, equipment manuals and manufacturer registrations in the property file so you can find them when you need them.

sections.h2: What are the warning signs of a problem contractor?
sections.body:
Most contractor problems show early signs. Watch for these during bidding and early in the project.

During bidding:
- Reluctance to provide license and insurance documentation, or providing it only as a photocopy
- A bid that is a single number with no breakdown, or a scope that is vaguer than the one you provided
- Pressure for a large upfront payment or cash payment
- Suggestions to skip permits to save time or money
- A price far below other bids without a clear explanation
- No written contract, or a contract without a scope, schedule, payment terms or warranty
- Unwillingness to provide references from similar projects

During the project:
- Missed start dates and frequent unexplained absences from the site
- Progress reports that stop or become vague
- Draw requests ahead of completed work
- Pressure to approve change orders verbally or without documentation
- Reluctance to provide lien waivers
- Failed inspections that are not explained or corrected promptly
- Subcontractors or suppliers contacting you about non-payment

When you see these signs, act early. Address the issue in writing, refer to the contract, and stop advancing payment beyond verified work. If problems continue, consult your contract's dispute and termination provisions and get advice appropriate to your situation.

The best prevention is the process described in this guide: a detailed scope, verified credentials, payment tied to completed work, lien waivers with every draw, regular documented communication and a written warranty. Contractors who work well with investors welcome that structure because it protects them too.

faqs.q: How many bids should I get for a rehab?
faqs.a: Enough to understand the range of pricing and approach for your scope, which for many investors means a few qualified contractors. More important than the number is that every bidder prices the same written scope with the same allowances and exclusions. Three bids on three different interpretations of the work tell you less than two bids on one clear scope. Once you find a contractor who performs well, repeat work often matters more than re-bidding every job.

faqs.q: Should I pay a contractor a deposit?
faqs.a: Keep deposits modest and tied to specific purposes such as special-order materials, and check whether your state limits home improvement deposits. Avoid large upfront payments that leave you exposed if the contractor does not perform. A sound structure pays draws as work is completed and verified, collects lien waivers with each payment, and holds final payment until the work is finished, inspected and accepted. Some investor-focused contractors require no upfront payment at all.

faqs.q: What is a lien waiver and why do I need one?
faqs.a: A lien waiver is a document in which a contractor, subcontractor or supplier gives up the right to file a lien against your property for amounts that have been paid. In many states, unpaid subcontractors and suppliers can file liens even if you paid the general contractor in full. Collecting waivers with each draw, and final waivers at completion, protects your title, keeps your lender comfortable and prevents problems at sale or refinance.

faqs.q: How do I manage a rehab when I am not local?
faqs.a: Remote rehabs depend on process. Hire a contractor with a designated project manager who visits the site regularly. Agree on a reporting cadence with photos and video, including documentation before walls are closed. Tie payments to verified milestones, using your lender's inspector, a third-party inspector, or detailed photos. Make decisions in writing and respond quickly. Keep permits, lien waivers and warranties in a shared project file you can access from anywhere.

faqs.q: What should be in a renovation contract?
faqs.a: At minimum: the parties, property address, a detailed scope or reference to an attached scope document, allowances and exclusions, the price and payment schedule tied to milestones, the start and completion dates, the change-order process, permit responsibility, insurance requirements, lien waiver requirements, warranty terms, and how disputes and termination are handled. Your state may require specific contract terms for home improvement work, and your attorney can advise on what fits your situation.
